# **How to make a schema**

This guide serves to partially document how the tbl part of the tool works in a more comprehensive fashion and to allow people into the future to add support for their own files or support for more obscure versions of Kuro no Kiseki. As this guide mostly serves for advanced users, the guide will also assume that you have some amount of rudimentary knowledge of hex editing.

# **Requirements**

* Pyhton version 3,10 and up (something you've probably already installed if you’ve looked at this guide)  
   	  
* Notepad++ : [https\://notepad-plus-plus.org/downloads/](https://notepad-plus-plus.org/downloads/)  
   	  
* IDLE  (comes packaged with Python)  
   	  
* HxD: [https\://mh-nexus.de/en/hxd/](https://mh-nexus.de/en/hxd/)

Note : this guide will describe my method of doing this with these tools since they tend to serve as the current defaults. If you have another Python IDE, a different text editor than Notepad++ (as long as it has perfect alignment for characters) or a different hex editor than HxD, they should work just fine for this guide.

# **Step 1 : making file « files »**

For the purposes of this guide, I will be making a schema for t\_quartz\_line.tbl  
A bit of a confusing name for this section, but it's very simple actually.  
First of all, open the file you'd like to make a schema for inside your hex editor of choice.

What’s important on this screen for this first step is the text circled in red here (which are “ElementSlotRate” and “QuartzLineParam”). For each of these sets of text present here, to make a fully supported file, you’ll need to make a schema file. But we’re getting a bit ahead of ourselves here.  
Inside KuroTools, open up the “schemas” directory.  
![][image2]  
Inside this directory, copy and paste a new json file from this list and rename it the name of the file you’d like to make a schema of.

(I copy and pasted t\_books and rename it to t\_quartz\_line here)  
Next, open up the new file and edit it so that it has the name of every single “header” that we talked about inside in the correct format:

(make sure there is a comma at the end of every line except the last header of the list)

# Step 2: Making the schema

Now for the actual hard part: documenting what every value within the header is.  
Let’s start off by making a schema for “ElementSlotRate” (which also happens to be an extremely simple schema).  
So, after doing the first step, head into the “headers” directory.  
![][image6]  
Copy and paste one of these (I recommend using ActiveVoiceTableData for this, but use whichever one you want for this) and rename it to the name of the header you want to make a schema for.   
![][image7]  
Note: if your header is already on this list, you’ll need to add a schema to an already existing file and make a new version of it so that it supports your version of the game (check out the structure of a schema like “QuestTitle” which needs a schema for the Falcom JP PS4 version and another for the CLE PC version to see how to do this)

Open up your new file  
![][image8]  
We need to fill in the data for what the schema does.  
To do this, we will need to document what’s in your hex editor.  
![][image9]This highlighted value right here indicates the starting position of your schema.  
Note: Trails uses Little Endian, so the hex offset indicated by this value will be reversed from the one shown in your hex editor (so, hex offset E8 03 means that it will be hex offset 3E8 in your hex editor)  
![][image10]This one indicates the length of each entry of the header.  
![][image11]This final one that we will need here indicates how many entries of that header are in the file.  
At only a single entry and 4 values, ElementSlotRate is going to have an extremely simple and short schema to create.

We can find all the data for ElementSlotRate starting hex offset A8:  
![][image12]Since this schema is brutally short this is the only data we have inside this schema we need to transcribe. Head back to your json that you named your header for and transcribe your data.  
Before:  
![][image13]  
After:  
![][image14]  
Relative to other schemas, this schema is unusually simple to the point I skipped each step.  
The “slot\_restriction\_multiplier” is what I’ll be naming this variable since this section controls the amount elementals of a quartz are multiplied by when placed into this restriction (the float above is equal to 2).  
This second part defines this value as a “float” (something which I’ll explain in a second)  
After doing a simple case study, let’s move on to a much larger and more standard schema.

# Step 3: Making a more complicated schema

This time, I will be making a schema for the second header of t\_quartz\_line: QuartzLineParam and how to do that.  
Just as in the last step, create a new file in the headers directory pertaining to your new header and open it in Notepad++  
![][image15]  
Grab once again the data pertaining to the header from your hex editor like last time![][image16]  
(in this case, the header starts at hex offset 0xAC, each entry has a length of 40 values and there are 80 entries)  
Note: the following is simply how I do this process, feel free to take any liberties of your own in terms of method as long as it works.  
Copy and paste the data for the first entry into a new blank Notepad++ document:  
![][image17]  
![][image18]  
Next, copy and paste the rest of the entries of the header onto a second line:  
![][image19]  
The final step is to add a line break at the end of every entry. The quickest way of doing this without taking an insane amount of time is to:

1. Add an extra space at the end of the first line:

![][image20]

2. Head to the beginning of the second line  
3. Press the Left Arrow Key, then the Down Arrow Key and then Enter in quick succession over and over.

Note: the goal is to have a reasonable enough sample size to compare entries to input data correctly. If your file has over 1k entries, about 100 should be more than enough to do this job.  
At the end, you’ll want a text file filled with hex data that’s aligned correctly that looks something like this:  
![][image21]This will allow us to compare the values of each entry and see what is what.  
Head back to our schema file for this header we created earlier in the schemas/headers directory.  
![][image22]  
We need to modify these values and entries right here to match the data of the header we’re making.  
Here are the types of values you can input (in brackets at the end are the length of each value in hex):  
“byte”: An 8-bit value going from \-128 to 127 (1)  
“short”: A 16-bit value going from \-32768 to 32767 (2)  
“int”: A 32-bit value going from \-2147483648 to 2147483647 (4)  
“long”: A 64-bit value going from \-9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807 (8)  
“ubyte”: An unsigned 8-bit value going from 0 to 255 (1)  
“ushort”: An unsigned 16-bit balue going from 0 to 65535 (2)  
“uint”: An unsigned 32-bit value going from 0 to 4294967295 (4)  
“ulong”: An unsigned 64-bit value going 0 to 18446744073709551615 (8)  
“toffset”: a 64-bit hex offset that is a pointer pointing to text somewhere else in the file (8)  
“float”: a 32-bit value used for decimal points (4)  
“u16array”: a 64-bit hex offset followed by an integer. The hex offset points to sets of “short” values to be read at a specified offset. The amount of short values read is determined by the integer following it (12)  
“u32array”: a 64-bit hex offset followed by an integer. The hex offset points to sets of “int” values to be read at a specified offset. The amount of int values read is determined by the integer following it (12)  
Note: “u8array” and “u64array” are implemented into the program but have no currently known use cases.

Using these value types, I modify the header to list in sequence what values to read.  
Note: since checking whether every value is unsigned or not is either a pain in the neck or impossible (since you might be making a schema for values you don’t even know the meaning of) I’d use as a rule of thumb to use unsigned for bytes and shorts by default and signed for int and long values since their caps are large enough that conflicts tend to be rare even if you’re wrong.

After this, modify and make your schema:  
![][image23]  
This is the end result for the schema I was making comparing all the values.  
If you don’t know what the values actually do in-game, name them in a sort of generic fashion as seen above.

# Step 4: Testing your schema

Finally, you need to test the schema you’re making.  
To test it, drag and drop the game file you just made a schema for onto the “tbl2json” script and if it decompiles into a json, congrats\! (for the most part, you still need to do one last part)  
If not, then you have some debugging to do.  
Open up IDLE (or any Python IDE of your choice) and run the script.   
In IDLE, put the tbl file into the KuroTools directory and then:

1. Open up the “tbl2json” script in IDLE  
2. Then go to “Run\>Run… Customized”  
3. Input for argument the name of the tbl file you want to decompile

For example: “t\_quartz\_line.tbl”  
The 2 most common errors are:

- The length of the schema is incorrect causing the file to not decompile. This error is particularly nasty because, while no file is generated, the IDE also doesn’t give any error text.  
  - Edit: It now gives out a key error equal to the length of the missing schema length now.  
- Forgetting a comma or putting one where it shouldn’t be at the end of a line

# Step 5: Making sure recompiled files are correct

If your file has text inside or uses one of the array pointers (like u16array), then make sure that you’ve pointed to all the text inside your file.  
This is crucial, because the IDE isn’t going to give you an error on this, your file will decompile and recompile just fine (probably) but the tool will be making files with bogus text or even worse, game crashes.
